title: Photosynthesis Impostor
briefing: Everyone gets a fact card about the round's topic, but one card is secretly wrong. Read yours aloud, explain why it's true, grill weak explanations, then vote out the impostor.
intro: Five rounds, from pigments to C4 plants. Each round, one player's card has been corrupted with a classic photosynthesis misconception.
outro_win: The crew caught the impostors. Your understanding of photosynthesis held up under cross-examination.
outro_lose: The impostors slipped through. Review each round's fake and why it's wrong, then play again.

true_facts: Pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes, grouped with proteins into light-harvesting complexes around each photosystem.
Accessory pigments like chlorophyll b and carotenoids pass the energy they absorb along to reaction-center chlorophyll a.
When a pigment molecule absorbs a photon, one of its electrons is boosted up to a higher energy level.
Carotenoids widen the range of usable light and also protect chlorophyll from damage by excess light.
In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down first, revealing yellow and orange carotenoids that were in the leaf all along.
Isolated chlorophyll in a test tube glows red because its excited electrons fall back with no acceptor to catch them.
Light energy becomes chemical energy only when the reaction-center chlorophyll hands an excited electron to an acceptor.
Having several different pigments lets a leaf capture a wider band of wavelengths than chlorophyll a could alone.
Photosystem II's reaction center is called P680 because its chlorophyll absorbs best at 680 nanometers.
Up to a saturation point, brighter light excites more electrons per second and speeds up the light reactions.
rounds.corrupted_fact: Leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs green light most strongly and uses it to power photosynthesis.
rounds.correct_version: Leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly and reflects most of the green light.
rounds.explanation: The color you see is the light a pigment does NOT absorb. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue best; green bounces back to your eyes.

rounds.topic: Electron flow in the light reactions
true_facts: Photosystem II passes its excited electrons to plastoquinone, which carries them through the thylakoid membrane.
As electrons pass through the cytochrome complex, their energy is used to pump H+ into the thylakoid lumen.
Photosystem I re-energizes electrons with a second photon so they have enough energy to reduce NADP+.
At the end of the chain, NADP+ reductase adds two electrons and an H+ to NADP+ to form NADPH.
In linear electron flow, electrons travel from Photosystem II to Photosystem I, never the other way around.
Plastocyanin is a small copper protein that ferries electrons from the cytochrome complex to Photosystem I.
In cyclic electron flow, Photosystem I sends electrons back to the cytochrome complex, making ATP but no NADPH.
The light reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes, while the Calvin cycle happens in the stroma.
Electrons lose a little energy at each step of the transport chain, like a ball bouncing down a staircase.
The herbicide DCMU blocks electrons from leaving Photosystem II, so NADPH production in the leaf stops.
rounds.corrupted_fact: The oxygen gas released during photosynthesis comes from splitting carbon dioxide molecules in the Calvin cycle.
rounds.correct_version: The oxygen gas released during photosynthesis comes from splitting water molecules at Photosystem II.
rounds.explanation: Isotope tracer experiments show that labeled oxygen in water, not in CO2, ends up in the O2 gas. CO2's oxygen ends up in sugar and water.

true_facts: In bright light the thylakoid lumen can reach about pH 5, while the stroma stays near pH 8.
The H+ gradient across the thylakoid membrane stores potential energy, like water held behind a dam.
ATP synthase is a rotary enzyme whose spinning part is turned by the flow of hydrogen ions through it.
Chemiosmosis in chloroplasts works on the same principle as ATP production in mitochondria.
Splitting water on the lumen side of the membrane releases H+ into the lumen, adding to the gradient.
If the thylakoid membrane is made leaky to H+, electron transport can continue but ATP production drops.
The cytochrome complex uses energy from passing electrons to pump H+ across the thylakoid membrane.
ATP made by chloroplast ATP synthase is released into the stroma, right where the Calvin cycle uses it.
Linear electron flow alone makes slightly too little ATP for the Calvin cycle, so cyclic flow tops it up.
Forming NADPH on the stroma side removes H+ there, which makes the gradient across the membrane steeper.
rounds.corrupted_fact: ATP synthase makes ATP as H+ ions flow from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen, down their gradient.
rounds.correct_version: ATP synthase makes ATP as hydrogen ions flow from the thylakoid lumen out into the stroma, down their gradient.
rounds.explanation: H+ is pumped INTO the lumen, so the lumen is the high-concentration side. ATP synthase is driven as H+ flows back OUT to the stroma.

true_facts: In the fixation step, Rubisco attaches CO2 to a five-carbon sugar called RuBP.
The unstable six-carbon product of fixation immediately splits into two three-carbon molecules of 3-PGA.
In the reduction step, ATP and NADPH from the light reactions convert 3-PGA into G3P.
For every three CO2 molecules fixed, the cycle makes six G3P but exports only one as net sugar.
Five of every six G3P molecules are rearranged, using more ATP, to rebuild RuBP.
Building one net G3P from three CO2 costs the cycle 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.
G3P exported from the chloroplast can be built into glucose, sucrose, starch, or even amino acids.
The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma, the fluid that surrounds the thylakoids.
Without RuBP regeneration, fixation would stop quickly because Rubisco would run out of its CO2 acceptor.
Almost all the carbon in a tree's wood originally came from CO2 taken in through its leaves.
rounds.corrupted_fact: The Calvin cycle runs mainly at night, when the light reactions stop and the plant is free to fix CO2.
rounds.correct_version: The Calvin cycle runs mainly during the day, because it depends on the ATP and NADPH the light reactions make.
rounds.explanation: The old name 'dark reactions' only means they don't use light directly. They need a constant supply of ATP and NADPH, which stops soon after dark.

true_facts: Rubisco can bind O2 instead of CO2, and it does so more often as leaf temperature rises.
Photorespiration uses up ATP and releases CO2 without producing any sugar.
When stomata close on a hot, dry day, O2 builds up inside the leaf and CO2 runs low.
PEP carboxylase grabs CO2 even at very low concentrations and never binds O2 by mistake.
CAM plants such as cacti open their stomata at night and store CO2 as organic acids until daytime.
CAM plants separate CO2 capture and the Calvin cycle in time, while C4 plants separate them in space.
At low light, adding more CO2 barely raises the photosynthesis rate, because light is the limiting factor.
Above an optimum temperature, the photosynthesis rate falls as enzymes like Rubisco start to lose their shape.
C4 plants spend extra ATP to concentrate CO2, which pays off in hot climates but not in cool ones.
Rubisco is so slow that plants make huge amounts of it, making it likely the most abundant protein on Earth.
rounds.corrupted_fact: In C4 plants, Rubisco works in the mesophyll cells, right where PEP carboxylase first captures the CO2.
rounds.correct_version: In C4 plants, Rubisco works in the bundle-sheath cells, where CO2 first captured by PEP carboxylase in the mesophyll is concentrated.
rounds.explanation: C4 plants separate the two enzymes in space: PEP carboxylase captures CO2 in the mesophyll, then it is shuttled to bundle-sheath cells so Rubisco sees high CO2 and little O2.
